title: Chapter 24 — Causes Which Render Democratic Armies Weaker Than Other Armies At The Outset Of A Campaign, And More Formidable In Protracted Warfare
paragraphs: Armies at the Outset of a Campaign, and More Formidable in Protracted Warfare

After a long peace, any army is in danger of being beaten at the start of a campaign, and any army that has been at war for a long time has a strong chance of victory. This truth applies with particular force to democratic armies. In aristocracies the military is a privileged career and is honored even in peacetime. Men of great talent, great accomplishments and great ambition enter it, and the army is in every respect level with the nation and often above it. We have seen, by contrast, that among a democratic people the better minds of the nation are gradually drawn away from the military profession to seek distinction, power and especially wealth by other paths. After a long peace (and in democratic ages periods of peace are long), the army is always inferior to the country itself. In this state it is called into active service, and until war has changed it, the country is in danger as well as the army.

I have shown that in democratic armies in peacetime, seniority is the supreme and inflexible rule of advancement. As I noted earlier, this follows not only from the structure of these armies but from the nature of the people, and it will always be so. Also, because an officer in these nations gets his standing in the country entirely from his standing in the army, and draws from the same source all the distinction and comfortable means he enjoys, he does not leave his profession, or get retired for age, until very near the end of his life. The result of these two causes is that when a democratic people goes to war after a long stretch of peace, all the leading officers of the army are old men. I speak not only of the generals but of the non-commissioned officers, most of whom have stood still or advanced only step by step. One may notice with surprise that in a democratic army after a long peace all the soldiers are mere boys and all the senior officers are in their declining years, so that the former lack experience and the latter lack vigor. This is a strong element of defeat, for the first condition of successful generalship is youth. I would not have ventured to say so if the greatest captain of modern times had not made the observation. These two causes do not act in the same way on aristocratic armies. Men there are promoted by right of birth far more than by seniority, so at every rank there are a certain number of young men who bring to their profession the full early vigor of body and mind. Also, since the men who seek military honors among an aristocratic people hold a settled position in civil society, they seldom stay in the army until old age overtakes them. After giving the most vigorous years of their youth to the career of arms, they retire of their own accord and spend the rest of their mature years at home.

A long peace not only fills democratic armies with elderly officers; it also gives all the officers habits of body and mind that make them unfit for real service. A man who has lived long in the calm, lukewarm atmosphere of democratic customs adapts poorly, at first, to the harder labors and sterner duties of war. If he has not entirely lost his taste for arms, he has at least taken up a way of life that unfits him for conquest.

Among aristocratic nations the comforts of civil life have less influence on the customs of the army, because there the aristocracy commands the army. An aristocracy, however deeply sunk in luxurious pleasures, always has many other passions besides its own well-being, and it will readily sacrifice that well-being to satisfy those passions more fully. *a

I have shown that in democratic armies in peacetime promotion is extremely slow. At first the officers bear this state of affairs impatiently. They grow excited, restless and exasperated, but in the end most of them resign themselves to it. Those with the most ambition and the most resources leave the army. The others adjust their tastes and desires to their small fortunes and eventually come to view the military profession from a civilian standpoint. The quality they value most in it is the comfortable means and security that go with it. Their whole idea of the future rests on the certainty of this modest provision, and all they ask is to enjoy it in peace. So a long peace not only fills an army with old men; it often gives the outlook of old men to those who are still in their prime.

I have also shown that among democratic nations in peacetime the military profession is held in little honor and followed without much zeal. This lack of public favor is a heavy discouragement to the army. It weighs on the spirits of the troops, and when war finally breaks out, they cannot at once recover their spring and vigor. Aristocratic armies have no comparable cause of moral weakness. Their officers are never lowered in their own eyes or in their countrymen’s, because, apart from their military greatness, they are personally great. But even if peace affected the two kinds of armies in the same way, the results would still differ. When the officers of an aristocratic army have lost their warlike spirit and their desire to rise through service, they still keep a certain respect for the honor of their class and an old habit of being the first to set an example. But when the officers of a democratic army no longer have the love of war and the ambition of arms, nothing at all is left to them.

I am therefore of the opinion that when a democratic people goes to war after a long peace, it runs a much greater risk of defeat than any other nation. But it should not be easily discouraged by its reverses, because the chances of success for such an army increase as the war goes on. When a war has at last, by its long duration, roused the whole community from its peaceful occupations and ruined its small undertakings, the same passions that made the people attach so much importance to keeping the peace will turn to arms. After war has destroyed every other kind of speculation, it becomes itself the great and only speculation, and all the ardent and ambitious desires that equality produces are directed to it alone. This is why the very same democratic nations that are so reluctant to go to war sometimes accomplish prodigious feats once they have taken the field. As the war draws more and more of the public’s attention, and is seen to make great reputations and great fortunes in a short time, the best spirits of the nation enter the military profession. All the enterprising, proud and martial minds, no longer of the aristocracy alone but of the whole country, are drawn in this direction. The number of competitors for military honors is huge, and war sends every man to his proper level, so great generals are sure to emerge. A long war has the same effect on a democratic army that a revolution has on a people: it breaks through regulations and lets extraordinary men rise above the common level. The officers whose bodies and minds have aged in peace are removed, or retired for age, or die. In their place a host of young men press forward, whose frames are already hardened and whose desires have been widened and inflamed by active service. They are set on advancement at any cost, and on constant advancement. Behind them come others with the same passions and desires, and behind these still others, limited by nothing but the size of the army. The principle of equality opens the door of ambition to everyone, and death supplies the openings for ambition. Death constantly thins the ranks, creating vacancies, closing and opening the career of arms.

There is, moreover, a secret connection between the military character and the character of democracies, which war brings to light. The men of democracies are naturally passionate in their eagerness to get what they covet and to enjoy it on easy terms. For the most part they worship chance, and they fear death much less than they fear difficulty. This is the spirit they bring to commerce and manufacturing, and the same spirit, carried onto the battlefield, leads them to risk their lives willingly in order to win the rewards of victory in a moment. No kind of greatness appeals more to the imagination of a democratic people than military greatness, a greatness of vivid and sudden brilliance, won without toil by nothing but the risk of life. So while the interests and tastes of the members of a democratic community turn them away from war, their habits of mind fit them to wage it well. Once roused from their business and their pleasures, they soon make good soldiers. If peace is especially harmful to democratic armies, war gives them advantages that no other armies ever have, and these advantages, however little felt at first, cannot fail in the end to give them victory. An aristocratic nation that, in a contest with a democratic people, fails to ruin the latter at the outset of the war always runs a great risk of being conquered by it.
